Alright, the latest debugging run with dbg-bots.mjs has finally given me some concrete data. The console output shows four bots all in the “patrol” state, alive, and their positions are updating every second (e.g., path 3 pos [25.2,0,-22.6] → [25.4,0,-18.3] → [25.5,0,-13.7] … etc.). The FPS is also healthy (mid‑20s), and there are no errors reported. This tells me that, at least in a stripped‑down scenario where the bots are simply patrolling on an empty map with the graphics set to “potato”, the AI movement system is functioning correctly.

But earlier in the playtest report I still have those glaring failures:
- “bots navigate foundry” – 0/4 moved
- “bots navigate bastion” – 0/4 moved
- “bot AI spots and engages exposed player” – hp 100 after 10 sim‑s
- “HDR bloom visibly changes pixels”

Those navigation failures must be coming from a different part of the test harness, not from the core movement code itself. The test that checks navigation likely measures net displacement over a simulated‑time window while the bots are also trying to engage the player. If the bots enter an attack‑strafe loop (shooting while moving forward/backward) the net displacement could be near zero, causing the check to think they didn’t move at all, even though they are technically walking and shooting. That would also explain why the “engage” check reports the player still at full health after 10 sim‑seconds – perhaps the bots never actually close distance enough to deal damage because their movement is being cancelled out by the strafing logic.

Given that the isolated patrol test passes, the next logical step is to isolate the engagement scenario itself and see what the bots actually do when a player is present. I need to probe that specific case: spawn a player, let the bots detect and engage, and log their state, positions, and any damage dealt. If the bots are stuck in a zero‑net‑displacement loop, I’ll see that in the logs. If they’re simply not detecting the player, that will also become evident.

So I’ll tell the user what I’ve learned and propose the next diagnostic step: probing the engage scenario. That’s exactly what the message should convey.
